events.title: Roman Conquest of Pannonia
events.description: Roman Empire conquered western Hungary region, establishing Pannonia province. Romans built Danube frontier defense (Limes), constructing cities like Aquincum (today's Budapest), Sopron and Szekesfehervar. Roman rule brought urbanization, road networks, bathhouses and Christianity. Pannonia became important frontier province, defending against northern barbarians. Many Roman ruins preserved today, including amphitheaters and villas.

events.title: Soviet Invasion and Revolution Suppression
events.description: November 4 dawn, 200,000 Soviet troops and 2,500 tanks attacked Hungary. Nagy appealed to world for help via broadcast, then fled to Yugoslav embassy. Hungarian freedom fighters (including many youth and workers) desperately resisted with Molotov cocktails and light weapons, but outnumbered. Budapest fought fiercely for days, Corvin Cinema and Kilián Barracks became resistance symbols. November 10, organized resistance basically ended, but sporadic fighting continued to mid-November. About 2,500-3,000 Hungarians and 700 Soviet soldiers killed. Soviets installed Kádár János puppet government. About 200,000 Hungarians fled to West.

events.title: Twelve Days of Revolution
events.description: October 28 ceasefire, Soviet forces began withdrawing from Budapest. Hungary experienced brief freedom: multi-party system restored, press freedom, political prisoners released, revolutionary committees managed. Nagy formed coalition government, declared Hungary withdrawing from Warsaw Pact, declaring neutrality. Nation celebrated, believing revolution succeeded. But Soviets secretly decided to suppress. November 1, Soviet massive forces entered Hungary from Ukraine. November 3, Soviets tricked then arrested Hungarian military delegation. November 4 dawn, Soviets launched massive attack.

events.title: Hunnic Empire of Attila
events.description: Huns under Attila established powerful empire centered in Pannonia. Attila (406-453) called 'Scourge of God,' empire stretched from Central Asia to Gaul. Hunnic cavalry renowned, threatening Eastern and Western Roman Empires. Attila's court located in today's Hungary, attracting envoys from various peoples. But after Attila's death in 453, empire rapidly collapsed. Huns have no direct blood relation to today's Hungarian Magyars, but occupy important place in Hungarian national legend.

events.title: Avar Khaganate
events.description: Avars (nomadic people from Central Asia) conquered Pannonian Basin, establishing khaganate ruling about 250 years. Avars were elite cavalry, using stirrup technology. Their capital located in today's Hungary, conducting raids against Byzantium and Frankish Kingdom. Avar culture influenced later Magyars. Khaganate destroyed by Charlemagne in 796-803, Avars assimilated and disappeared. Archaeology discovered numerous Avar burials and treasures.

events.title: Magyar Conquest (Honfoglalás)
events.description: Magyar tribal confederation under Grand Prince Árpád migrated from Ural Mountains and Black Sea steppes, conquering Pannonian Basin. This is starting point of Hungarian history, called 'Conquest' (Honfoglalás). Magyars were Ugric-speaking nomadic people, alliance of seven tribes. They defeated local Slavic and Bulgar forces, settling in basin. Árpád founded dynasty ruling over 400 years. After conquest, Magyar cavalry conducted 'raids' (Kalandozások) into Western Europe, penetrating France, Italy and Byzantium, shocking Europe.

events.title: Battle of Lechfeld
events.description: German King Otto I decisively defeated Hungarian army at Lechfeld (near Augsburg), ending nearly century of Magyar raids into Western Europe. This crushing defeat forced Hungary to abandon nomadic raiding lifestyle, turning toward settlement, agriculture and Christianization. Battle marked turning point in Hungarian history: transformation from nomadic raiders to settled European kingdom. Hungarian leaders recognized necessity of integrating into Christian Europe for survival.

events.title: Grand Prince Géza's Reforms
events.description: Grand Prince Géza (r. 972-997) began systematic Christianization and Westernization policy of Hungary. He invited foreign missionaries, encouraged settled agriculture, built churches. Géza himself baptized (though also retained pagan customs), had son Stephen educated in Christianity. Géza established diplomatic relations with Holy Roman Empire and Byzantium. His reforms paved way for son Saint Stephen to establish Christian kingdom.

events.title: Coronation of Saint Stephen and Kingdom Establishment
events.description: Stephen I crowned King of Hungary on Christmas with blessing from Pope Sylvester II, establishing Kingdom of Hungary. Pope sent 'Holy Crown' (though today's Holy Crown of Saint Stephen partly from later period). Stephen (r. 997-1038) completed Christianization, established diocesan system, built monasteries and churches, promulgated laws. He suppressed pagan rebellions, unified kingdom. Stephen created administrative system, feudal system and royal estates. He was canonized in 1083, becoming Hungary's most important national symbol and patron saint. Saint Stephen transformed Hungary into permanent member of medieval Christian Europe.

events.title: Stephen I's Kingdom Organization
events.description: Saint Stephen established foundation structure of Hungarian Kingdom: set up ten dioceses (two archdioceses: Esztergom and Kalocsa), established monasteries, divided county (vármegye) administrative districts, established royal guards and military organization. He invited foreign knights, craftsmen and monks to settle. Promulgated 'Admonitions' to son Emeric, expounding Christian governance principles. Stephen used Latin as official language, adopted Western feudal system. He successfully consolidated royal power against tribal nobles, establishing centralization.

events.title: Succession Crisis and Pagan Rebellion
events.description: After Saint Stephen's death without legitimate son (son Emeric died early), throne succession caused crisis. Peter Orseolo (Venetian) and Samuel Aba successively ruled, but in 1046 large-scale pagan rebellion erupted (Vata uprising). Rebels killed bishops, destroyed churches, attempted to restore paganism. Rebellion suppressed, Andrew I (Árpád family) took throne, Christian rule finally consolidated. This was Hungary's last pagan restoration attempt.

events.title: Saint Ladislaus's Reign
events.description: Ladislaus I (1077-1095) was one of greatest medieval Hungarian rulers. He repelled Cuman invasions, conquered Croatia and Dalmatia, expanding kingdom territory. Ladislaus consolidated Christianity, established strict laws (Code of Ladislaus), combating crime and heresy. He supported church reform, built monasteries. Ladislaus was exemplar of chivalry, canonized in 1192. His reign marked consolidation of Hungarian Kingdom and first golden age.

events.title: Wise Reign of King Coloman
events.description: Coloman 'the Book-lover' (Könyves Kálmán, 1095-1116) famous for learning, possibly former monk. He consolidated rule over Croatia, obtaining Croatian crown (1102). Coloman conducted legal reforms, codified laws, banned witch trials (extremely progressive in Europe). He declared 'witches do not exist.' Coloman supported culture and education, conducted diplomacy with Byzantium and Venice. His reign was period of Hungarian cultural flourishing.

events.title: Géza II and Byzantine Conflicts
events.description: During Géza II's reign (1141-1162), Hungary fought multiple wars with Byzantine Empire, contesting Balkan influence. Hungary supported Serbia against Byzantium. Géza also invited numerous foreign immigrants: Germans, Flemish and Walloons settled in Transylvania (Saxons), Jász and Cuman steppe dwellers. These immigrants received privileges, enriching kingdom's culture and economy.

events.title: Béla III's Prosperity
events.description: Béla III (1172-1196) grew up in Byzantine court, bringing Greek cultural influence. He was one of wealthiest European monarchs of Middle Ages, income exceeding French and English kings. Béla established efficient tax system, developed trade, minted high-quality silver coins. He built magnificent Esztergom and Buda palaces, patronized Gothic architecture. Béla rebuilt royal chancery, codified laws. His court was cultural center, attracting troubadours and scholars. This was Árpád dynasty's zenith.

events.title: Golden Bull
events.description: Andrew II was forced by nobles to issue the Golden Bull (Aranybulla), Hungary's 'Magna Carta' limiting royal power and guaranteeing noble rights. Bull stipulated king could not arbitrarily confiscate noble property, could not tax nobles, must summon parliament annually, nobles had right to resist tyranny. This established Hungarian noble privilege tradition, weakening centralization but also protecting from despotism. Golden Bull was one of important constitutional documents of medieval Europe, influencing Hungarian politics for centuries.

events.title: Béla IV's Rebuilding
events.description: Béla IV (1235-1270) ruled through Mongol disaster but worked to rebuild kingdom. He was called 'Second Founder' for reorganizing state after Mongol destruction. Béla invited Cumans to settle to replenish population, built stone castles for defense (previously mostly wood), developed cities and trade. But his civil war with son Stephen (later Stephen V) weakened kingdom, strengthening noble power.

events.title: Mongol Invasion and Catastrophe
events.description: Mongol Empire's Batu led massive army invading Hungary, one of greatest disasters in Hungarian history. On April 11, 1241 Mongols won great victory at Battle of Mohi, destroying Hungarian army. Mongol forces swept across country, massacring hundreds of thousands (population loss estimated 25-50%), destroying towns and monasteries. Béla IV fled to Dalmatia. In 1242 Mongols withdrew due to death of Ögedei Khan, Hungary spared from complete conquest. But state suffered unprecedented destruction, requiring decades to recover. Disaster exposed Hungarian defense weaknesses, prompting construction of stone fortresses.

events.title: Extinction of Árpád Dynasty
events.description: Andrew III died without heir, Árpád dynasty that ruled Hungary over 400 years extinct. This opened prolonged succession struggle, multiple foreign dynasties claiming inheritance: Bohemia, Bavaria and Angevin of Naples. Eventually Charles Robert of Anjou won, opening Angevin dynasty. But Árpád dynasty's end marked termination of Hungarian national dynasty, subsequent kings mostly of foreign origin.

events.title: Charles I's Centralization
events.description: Charles Robert (Charles I, 1308-1342) after years of civil war secured throne, began restoring royal power. He attacked powerful oligarch nobles, confiscated their castles, rebuilt royal estates. Charles reformed finances, introduced gold florin currency, developed gold mines (Hungary was Europe's major gold producer), promoted trade. He established dynastic alliances with Poland and Naples. Charles restored kingdom's order and prosperity.

events.title: Louis the Great's Golden Age
events.description: Louis I 'the Great' (1342-1382) was one of Hungary's greatest monarchs, his reign was zenith of Hungarian power. He inherited Polish throne (1370), ruling both countries forming great alliance. Louis expanded into Balkans, conquered Naples multiple times (briefly), war with Venice, controlled Dalmatia. He patronized culture, planned university establishment, built magnificent palaces and churches. Louis strengthened noble privileges (1351 decree confirmed Golden Bull) but maintained royal power balance. His court was one of Europe's most splendid. Hungarian territory reached maximum, from Adriatic Sea to Black Sea.

events.title: Sigismund's Reign
events.description: Sigismund (1387-1437) of Luxembourg dynasty became King of Hungary, Holy Roman Emperor and King of Bohemia. His long reign faced many challenges: 1396 Crusade of Nicopolis crushed by Ottomans, Hungarian noble rebellions, financial difficulties. But Sigismund was outstanding diplomat, convened Council of Constance, played central role in European politics. He strengthened Hungary's southern defenses against Ottomans, developed economy, promoted Renaissance culture.

events.title: Crusade of Nicopolis Defeat
events.description: Large crusade led by Sigismund (including Hungarian, French, English, Polish knights) was thoroughly defeated by Ottoman Sultan Bayezid I at Nicopolis (today's Bulgaria). This was last large medieval crusade, its failure shocked Christian Europe. Thousands of knights killed or captured. Crushing defeat marked Ottomans could not be stopped, Hungary became frontline against Ottoman expansion.

events.title: Budai Nagy Antal Revolt and Transylvanian Union
events.description: Large peasant uprising erupted in Transylvania (Budai Nagy Antal Revolt), composed of Vlachs and Hungarian peasants opposing noble oppression and serfdom. Revolt bloodily suppressed. In response, Transylvania's three privileged estates (Hungarian nobles, Székelys and Saxons) formed 'Union of Three Nations' (Unio Trium Nationum), excluding Romanian peasants, consolidating privileges. This deepened social and ethnic divisions.

events.title: Varna Crusade and János Hunyadi's Rise
events.description: Polish-Hungarian King Władysław III (Ulászló I) with General János Hunyadi led 'Long Campaign' counterattacking Ottomans, achieving some victories. But in 1444 at Battle of Varna, allied forces defeated by Sultan Murad II, king killed. János Hunyadi survived, becoming Hungary's regent and chief general, continuing to fight Ottomans for decades, becoming legendary hero.

events.title: Siege of Belgrade
events.description: Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II (just conquered Constantinople) led massive army besieging Belgrade, intending to open gate to Hungary. János Hunyadi led Hungarian army and crusader peasants organized by Franciscan monk John of Capistrano to break siege. After fierce battle on July 21-22, Ottomans repelled, this was major victory for Christian world. Pope Callixtus III ordered noon bells to commemorate victory (some places maintain today). But Hunyadi died shortly after from plague.

events.title: King Matthias's Renaissance
events.description: Matthias Corvinus (Matthias I, 1458-1490), son of János Hunyadi, was Hungary's greatest and most beloved king. He was military genius, established Black Army (Europe's first standing mercenary army), defeated Ottomans, Bohemia and Holy Roman Empire, conquered Vienna (1485) and Moravia. Matthias was Renaissance prince, established Bibliotheca Corviniana (one of Europe's largest libraries), patronized humanists, brought Italian Renaissance to Hungary. His Buda palace famous for luxury. Matthias reformed administration and judiciary, strengthened centralization but conflicted with nobles. In folk legend he embodies justice and wisdom.

events.title: Jagiellon Dynasty Decline
events.description: After Matthias died without legitimate heir, Vladislaus II (Ulászló II, 1490-1516) of Polish Jagiellon dynasty elected king. But he was called 'Dobzse László' (King Okay) because he always said okay to noble demands, weak king. Nobles seized power, royal authority collapsed, peasant burdens increased. 1514 massive peasant uprising (Dózsa Revolt) brutally suppressed, leading to harsher serf laws. State military weakened, finances chaotic, unable to resist Ottoman threat. Young Louis II (1516-1526) inherited facing disaster.

events.title: György Dózsa Peasant Uprising
events.description: Székely noble György Dózsa led massive peasant crusade uprising, originally meant against Ottomans but turned against Hungarian nobles oppressing them. Tens of thousands of peasants attacked noble estates, burned castles. Noble army suppressed uprising with extreme cruelty: Dózsa subjected to 'iron throne' torture (seated on red-hot iron chair, wearing red-hot iron crown). After uprising, 1514 law permanently bound peasants to land (complete serfdom), depriving freedom of movement. This deepened social divisions, weakened state's ability to resist foreign enemies.

events.title: Succession Struggle and Tripartite Hungary
events.description: After Mohács, two kings elected: Ferdinand of Austria (Habsburg) and Transylvanian noble John Zápolya. Both sides civil war, Ottomans intervened. In 1541 Suleiman occupied Buda, Hungary officially split into three parts: central directly ruled by Ottomans (Buda Eyalet), western and northern controlled by Habsburgs ('Royal Hungary'), eastern became semi-independent Principality of Transylvania (Ottoman vassal but with autonomy). This division lasted 150 years.

events.title: Battle of Mohács and Kingdom Collapse
events.description: 20-year-old Louis II led Hungarian army at Mohács against massive Ottoman army led by Suleiman the Magnificent. Due to noble divisions, insufficient troops and tactical errors, Hungary completely crushed in less than two hours. About 15,000-20,000 Hungarians killed, including King Louis (drowned in swamp during retreat), seven bishops and most nobles. This was greatest disaster in Hungarian history, marking end of medieval Hungarian Kingdom. Country split into three parts, losing independence for centuries. Mohács became symbol of national tragedy.

events.title: Ottoman Occupation Period
events.description: Central Hungary under Ottoman rule about 150 years. Buda became pasha's seat. Ottomans converted mosques from churches, built bathhouses (today's Budapest thermal baths partly originate from this). Population greatly decreased, many areas abandoned. But Ottoman rule relatively tolerant, allowed Christian self-governance (millet system), taxation lighter than Habsburg zone. Border areas (Végvár) continuous warfare, fortresses constantly changed hands. Occupation profoundly changed Hungary, delayed development but also integrated multicultural influences.

events.title: Principality of Transylvania
events.description: Transylvania became semi-independent principality, nominally Ottoman vassal but actually had great autonomy. Principality under Zápolya, Báthory, Bethlen, Rákóczi families' rule became bastion of Hungarian culture and independence. Transylvania practiced religious tolerance (rare in contemporary Europe), recognizing Catholicism, Lutheranism, Calvinism and Unitarianism (four recognized religions). Principality conducted skillful diplomacy between Habsburg, Ottoman and Poland. Many Hungarian nobles viewed Transylvania as base for resisting Habsburg absolutism.

events.title: Bocskai István Uprising
events.description: Transylvanian Prince Bocskai István led uprising against Habsburgs, opposing religious oppression (Counter-Reformation) and absolutist rule. Bocskai received Ottoman support, even elected King of Hungary (though never crowned). Uprising forced Habsburgs to sign Peace of Vienna (1606), guaranteeing Hungarian noble rights and religious freedom, especially for Protestants. This was first successful uprising of Hungarian nobles against Habsburgs, establishing pattern of constitutional struggle.

events.title: Golden Age of Bethlen Gábor
events.description: Transylvanian Prince Bethlen Gábor (1613-1629) was outstanding statesman and military leader in Hungarian history. He supported Protestant camp in Thirty Years' War, fighting Habsburgs. Bethlen elected King of Hungary three times but failed to consolidate. He was Renaissance prince, patronizing culture and education, developing economy. Bethlen made Transylvania important European power, capital Gyulafehérvár (Alba Iulia) became cultural center. He maintained peace with Ottomans while supporting Hungarian independence.

events.title: Battle of Vienna
events.description: Ottoman Empire's Kara Mustafa led last major offensive into Europe, besieging Vienna. Habsburg forces (including many Hungarian soldiers) and relief army led by Polish King Sobieski decisively defeated Ottomans on September 12. This was turning point in European history: Ottomans began decline, Habsburgs began counteroffensive. For Hungary, this meant Ottoman occupation would end, but also meant falling completely under Habsburg control.

events.title: Liberation of Buda
events.description: After 145 years of Ottoman occupation, Holy League forces (Habsburg, Papal, Polish, Venetian and Hungarian troops) under Prince Charles of Lorraine reconquered Buda. After two and half months of siege, city fell. Reconquest of Buda had enormous symbolic significance, marking beginning of end of Ottoman rule in Hungary. But city suffered severe destruction, population greatly decreased, requiring decades to rebuild.

events.title: Treaty of Karlowitz
events.description: Treaty of Karlowitz ended Great Turkish War between Habsburgs and Ottomans. Ottomans ceded most of Hungary (except Temesvár) and Transylvania to Habsburgs. This formally ended over 150 years of Ottoman occupation. But 'liberation' became new foreign rule: Habsburgs viewed Hungary as conquered territory, not partner kingdom. This aroused strong Hungarian noble discontent, leading to Rákóczi uprising.

events.title: Rákóczi Ferenc II War of Independence
events.description: Transylvanian Prince Rákóczi Ferenc II led Hungary's last large-scale War of Independence against Habsburgs. Uprising conducted by Kuruc rebel forces, received widespread support from peasants and nobles. Rákóczi established provisional government, dethroned Habsburg dynasty in 1707. But lacking foreign support (French Louis XIV eventually stopped aid), uprising failed after Peace of Szatmár in 1711. Rákóczi went into exile in Ottoman Empire, died in Turkey. Though failed, uprising became symbol of Hungarian national independence, Rákóczi became national hero.

events.title: Habsburg Consolidation of Rule
events.description: After Rákóczi uprising failed, Habsburgs consolidated rule over Hungary. Peace of Szatmár (1711) promised to respect Hungarian constitution and noble rights, but actually Habsburgs strengthened absolutism. Hungary became empire's granary and source of soldiers, economy subordinated to Vienna interests. German and South Slav immigrants introduced to recolonize war-devastated areas, changing demographic structure. Hungarian Diet still existed but with limited powers. Charles VI issued Pragmatic Sanction, ensuring Habsburg female succession (paving way for Maria Theresa).

events.title: Era of Maria Theresa
events.description: During Empress Maria Theresa's reign, relations with Hungary improved. During War of Austrian Succession, Hungarian nobles loyally supported Empress at 1741 Pressburg Diet (legendary 'Vitam et Sanguinem' - Life and Blood), providing troops and funds. In return, Theresa respected Hungarian autonomy, frequently visited Hungary, viewing it as loyal kingdom. She conducted reforms: improved peasant conditions, established schools, developed economy. But she also promoted Germanization and centralization, causing later tensions.

events.title: Joseph II's Reforms and Resistance
events.description: Enlightened absolutist Joseph II pushed radical reforms: abolishing serfdom (1785), implementing religious tolerance, judicial reform, German as official language (replacing Latin). But he ignored Hungarian constitution, abolished Hungary's special status, tried to integrate it as ordinary imperial province. This aroused strong resistance from all Hungarian classes. Nobles refused cooperation, even threatened uprising. Joseph on deathbed (1790) forced to revoke most Hungarian reforms. But his serfdom reforms and religious tolerance had lasting impact.

events.title: National Awakening and Reform Era
events.description: This period was Hungarian national awakening and reform movement era. Intellectuals promoted Hungarian language revival (replacing Latin), developed national culture and historical consciousness. Reform nobles like Széchenyi István ('Greatest Hungarian', promoting modernization) and Kossuth Lajos (radical nationalist) led movement, demanding constitutional reform, serfdom abolition, Hungarian independence and national equality. Diet became reform center. But tensions intensified between reformers and conservatives, different nationalities (Hungarians vs Slovaks, Romanians, Croats).

events.title: Diet Reconvenes and Reform Movement Begins
events.description: In 1825, Hungarian Diet reconvened after 13-year suspension, marking official start of Reform Era. Count Széchenyi István announced donation of one year's income to establish Hungarian Academy of Sciences (founded 1830), inspiring noble patriotism. Diet became stage for debating reforms: constitution, serfdom, economic modernization, Hungarian language status. Széchenyi promoted practical reforms: Danube navigation, Chain Bridge (connecting Buda and Pest), racecourse. His motto 'Hungary was not, but will be' inspired a generation.

events.title: Outbreak of 1848 Revolution
events.description: Inspired by Paris February Revolution, revolution erupted in Budapest on March 15, 1848. Young radicals (poet Petőfi Sándor and youth) gathered at cafes, proclaimed 'National Song' and 'Twelve Points', demanding press freedom, parliament, national independence, serfdom abolition. Revolution proceeded peacefully, bloodlessly. Facing revolutionary pressure, Vienna court yielded, appointing Batthyány Lajos as prime minister, forming responsible government. Hungary gained broad autonomy. Diet passed 'April Laws', abolishing serfdom, establishing constitutional monarchy. This was first time in Hungarian history achieving national independence and modern constitution.

events.title: War of Independence
events.description: After suppressing Vienna revolution, Habsburgs turned to attack Hungary, demanding retraction of concessions. Hungary refused, War of Independence erupted. Kossuth led resistance, General Görgei Artúr commanded revolutionary army. Hungarian forces won victories in Spring Campaign, liberating most territory. On April 14, 1849, Kossuth at Debrecen declared Habsburg dynasty dethroned, proclaiming Hungarian independence. But ethnic conflicts (Croats, Romanians, Serbs supporting Habsburgs) and Russian Tsar Nicholas I sending 200,000 troops to intervene determined revolution's failure.

events.title: Absolutist Rule and Passive Resistance
events.description: After revolution failed, Emperor Franz Joseph imposed absolutist rule. Hungary lost autonomy, treated as conquered territory, divided into multiple directly ruled districts. German official language, strict censorship, police state. Baron Bach's bureaucratic rule ('Bach Hussars' - German officials) resented by Hungarians. Hungarians adopted passive resistance: refused cooperation, did not recognize government legitimacy. But 1859 and 1866 Austrian military defeats (against France and Prussia) forced Vienna to reconsider relations with Hungary, seeking reconciliation.

events.title: Surrender at Világos and Revolution Failure
events.description: Facing overwhelming Austro-Russian forces, General Görgei surrendered to Russian army at Világos (hoping Russia would be more lenient than Austria). Kossuth and revolutionary government went into exile. Habsburgs bloodily retaliated: executed 13 revolutionary generals (Arad Martyrs, October 6, 1849), thousands imprisoned or executed. Kossuth went into overseas exile, becoming international symbol of freedom fighter. Revolution failed but profoundly impacted Hungary: serfdom abolition retained, national consciousness strengthened, 1848 became core of national myth.

events.title: Austro-Hungarian Compromise and Dual Monarchy
events.description: After years of negotiation, 1867 Austro-Hungarian Compromise (Ausgleich) reached, creating Austria-Hungary dual monarchy. Hungary restored constitution and autonomy, equal sharing of monarch with Austria (Franz Joseph as Austrian Emperor and Hungarian King). Two countries had common foreign affairs, defense and finance, but each had parliament, government and internal affairs. On June 8, Franz Joseph and Elisabeth (Sisi, beloved by Hungarians) crowned King and Queen of Hungary in Buda. Compromise satisfied Hungarian noble demands, opening half century of prosperity. But compromise also meant Hungary ruling multinational territory (Croats, Slovaks, Romanians, Serbs), triggering ethnic conflicts.

events.title: Prosperity of Dual Monarchy Era
events.description: 1867-1914 was most prosperous period in modern Hungarian history. Rapid economic development: industrialization, railway construction, Budapest becoming metropolis (1896 Millennial celebrations, building Parliament, Heroes' Square, Metro). Population growth, cultural flourishing, Hungary became one of important European powers. Parliamentary system operated, though suffrage limited. But problems accumulated: ethnic conflicts (Hungarians only 50% yet pushed Magyarization policy, suppressing minority languages and cultures), social inequality, worker and peasant poverty, political corruption. These contradictions exploded in World War I.

events.title: Millennial Celebrations
events.description: In 1896, Hungary grandly celebrated thousandth anniversary of Magyar conquest of Pannonia. This was zenith of national pride and confidence. Budapest hosted Millennial Exhibition, built iconic structures: Heroes' Square (statues of seven conquest tribal chiefs and successive kings), Fisherman's Bastion, Vajdahunyad Castle, continent's first metro. Celebrations showcased Hungarian modernization achievements, but also displayed Magyar nationalism, ignoring other nationalities, deepening divisions. Millennial celebrations were climax of dual monarchy, but also foreshadowed its collapse.

events.title: World War I
events.description: Hungary as part of Austria-Hungary participated in World War I on Central Powers side. In 1914, Hungarians initially supported war (against traditional enemies Serbia and Russia). But war quickly became war of attrition, bringing massive casualties (about 600,000 Hungarian soldiers killed) and economic collapse. In autumn 1918, Austria-Hungary disintegrated, Hungarian minorities (Romanians, Slovaks, South Slavs) declared independence or joined neighboring countries. Hungary faced territorial loss and political revolution.

events.title: Aster Revolution and Independence
events.description: On October 31, 1918, Budapest erupted in 'Aster Revolution' (protesters wore asters), overthrowing union with Austria. Count Károlyi Mihály became prime minister, declaring complete Hungarian independence. New government announced democratic reforms but faced Entente pressure and territorial demands. On November 13, Belgrade Armistice acknowledged Entente occupation of large Hungarian territories. Károlyi government powerless to prevent territorial dismemberment, lost popular support.

events.title: White Terror
events.description: After Soviet Republic collapsed, right-wing forces led by Admiral Horthy Miklós launched 'White Terror', retaliating against communists and supporters (many Jews, as Kun and other leaders were Jewish). Thousands executed or imprisoned, tens of thousands fled. This was one of darkest periods in modern Hungarian history, planting seeds of anti-Semitism. In March 1920, Horthy elected by parliament as 'Regent', restoring kingdom system (but without king), beginning conservative authoritarian rule.

events.title: Hungarian Soviet Republic
events.description: On March 21, 1919, Communist Kun Béla led revolution, establishing Hungarian Soviet Republic (Europe's second communist regime after Russia). Regime pushed radical socialism: confiscated land, nationalized industry, established Red Army. But Kun regime faced internal and external pressure: Romanian, Czechoslovak and Yugoslav invasion, domestic opposition and peasant resistance. Red Army initially resisted but collapsed in August. Romanian army occupied Budapest (looting property). Soviet Republic lasted only 133 days but left deep trauma, triggering subsequent White Terror.

events.title: Horthy Era
events.description: Horthy Miklós ruled Hungary as Regent for 25 years. Regime was conservative authoritarianism: parliament existed but with limited power, elections manipulated, opposition suppressed. Society conservative, Catholic Church influential, landowners retained power, land reform limited. Diplomacy focused on revising Trianon, seeking alliance with Italy, later Nazi Germany. Economic difficulties, Great Depression severely hit. 1930s anti-Semitic legislation increased (1920 first anti-Jewish law, limiting Jewish university admission). But Horthy era also had cultural flourishing, Hungary maintained relative stability until WWII dragged it into catastrophe.

events.title: Treaty of Trianon
events.description: Treaty of Trianon was Hungary's WWI defeat peace treaty, greatest national trauma in Hungarian history. Hungary lost 72% territory and 64% population: Transylvania to Romania, Upper Hungary to Czechoslovakia, Croatia to Yugoslavia, Burgenland to Austria. About 3.3 million Hungarians became minorities in neighboring countries. Hungary degraded from great power to small country, from multinational kingdom to single-nation state. 'Trianon' became symbol of national tragedy and injustice, slogan 'Nem, nem, soha!' (No, no, never!) expressed rejection. Treaty revision became core objective of interwar Hungarian diplomacy.

events.title: Territorial Recoveries
events.description: With Nazi Germany support, Hungary partially recovered lost territories through 'Vienna Awards': 1938 recovered southern Upper Hungary from Czechoslovakia, 1940 recovered Northern Transylvania from Romania, 1941 recovered partial territory from Yugoslavia. These 'recoveries' received enthusiastic Hungarian welcome, Horthy rode into Košice on horseback. But price was close alliance with Nazi Germany, ultimately dragging Hungary into WWII catastrophe. Recovered territories lost again after war.

events.title: Participation in World War II
events.description: In 1941, Hungary joined Nazi Germany attacking Soviet Union (partly from anti-communist ideology, partly hoping to recover more lost territory). Hungary sent Second Army to Eastern Front, suffered devastating Soviet blow at Don River in 1943, about 200,000 soldiers casualties or captured. Horthy tried seeking peace with West, but Germany discovered. On March 19, 1944, Germany occupied Hungary, installed puppet government, preventing its withdrawal from war. Hungary came under complete Nazi control, beginning systematic persecution of Jews.

events.title: Holocaust of Jews
events.description: After German occupation, Hungarian Jews (about 800,000, Europe's largest surviving Jewish community) faced catastrophe. Adolf Eichmann organized deportation, Hungarian authorities cooperated. May-July 1944, about 437,000 Jews (mainly from provinces) deported to Auschwitz, most immediately gassed. Budapest Jews temporarily spared under international pressure (including heroic efforts of Swedish diplomat Wallenberg) and Horthy stopping deportations. But after Arrow Cross takeover, Budapest Jews also massacred. About 565,000 Hungarian Jews perished in Holocaust, one of greatest crimes in Hungarian history.

events.title: Horthy's Abdication and Arrow Cross
events.description: On October 15, 1944, Horthy attempted to declare armistice and withdraw from war, but Germany kidnapped his son, forcing Horthy to abdicate. Nazis installed extreme fascist Arrow Cross Party (led by Szálasi Ferenc) to govern. Arrow Cross implemented terror rule: mass slaughter of Jews (shot on Danube banks, bodies thrown into river), forced labor, supporting Germany to the last. Budapest descended into chaos and violence. Arrow Cross ruled only months but caused tens of thousands of deaths.

events.title: Brief Democracy and Coalition Government
events.description: Post-war initial period, Hungary attempted multi-party democracy. November 1945 free elections, Smallholders' Party won (57%), Communists only 17%. Formed coalition government including Smallholders, Social Democrats and Communists. 1946 abolished monarchy, declared republic. Hungary experienced worst hyperinflation in human history (1946), introduced new currency forint to stabilize economy. But Soviet occupation and Communists (led by Rákosi Mátyás, with Soviet support) gradually seized power: controlled Interior Ministry and secret police, arrested opposition, manipulated elections. 1947 Smallholders split, Prime Minister Nagy Ferenc fled. Democratic hope shattered.

events.title: Siege of Budapest
events.description: Soviet Red Army besieged Budapest, German and Hungarian forces stubbornly resisted, this was one of bloodiest urban battles in European WWII. Fighting lasted 102 days (December 26, 1944-February 13, 1945), entire city became ruins. About 38,000 civilians died, hundreds of thousands fled. Buda Castle almost completely destroyed, all Danube bridges blown up. Red Army paid heavy price capturing city. After liberation, Soviet soldiers conducted widespread looting and rape. Siege of Budapest became symbol of Hungarian WWII suffering.

events.title: Soviet Occupation and War's End
events.description: In April 1945, Soviet Red Army completely occupied all Hungarian territory, war ended for Hungary. Hungary paid heavy price: about 300,000 soldiers killed, about 600,000 civilians died (including Holocaust victims), Budapest and many cities became ruins, economy completely collapsed. Soviet occupation brought new suffering: looted factory equipment as reparations, forced labor, sent tens of thousands of Hungarians (including POWs) to Soviet labor camps (many never returned). Hungarian women suffered mass sexual violence. But war's end also brought hope, democratic parties formed provisional government.

events.title: Communist Dictatorship
events.description: After 1947, Communists established complete dictatorship. 1948 forced Social Democrats to merge, forming Hungarian Working People's Party (MDP). Rákosi as Stalin's faithful follower implemented terror rule: one-party dictatorship, secret police (ÁVH) terror, political trials and executions (including Communist internal opposition), hundreds of thousands imprisoned or sent to labor camps. Economy fully Sovietized: nationalization, collectivization, heavy industry priority, Stalinist planned economy. Religious persecution, Cardinal Mindszenty arrested and sentenced. Living standards declined, society fearful. But after Stalin's death in 1953, reform pressure increased.

events.title: Nagy Imre's First Term
events.description: In 1953, under Soviet new leadership pressure, reformist Nagy Imre replaced Rákosi as Prime Minister. Nagy pushed 'New Course' reforms: released political prisoners, stopped forced collectivization, increased consumer goods production, relaxed political control, acknowledged past errors. Reforms welcomed by people, bringing hope. But party Stalinists (Rákosi remained party secretary) resisted. In 1955, Soviet attitude changed, Nagy dismissed, expelled from party, reforms reversed. Disappointed Hungarians waited for opportunity.

events.title: Retaliation and Nagy's Execution
events.description: After revolution suppressed, Kádár regime retaliated. Thousands arrested, hundreds executed, thousands imprisoned. Nagy and companions tricked out of Yugoslav embassy then kidnapped to Romania, secretly tried. On June 16, 1958, Nagy and three companions executed (hanged), secretly buried. This shocked world, becoming symbol of communist brutality. Nagy became martyr, 1956 Revolution became symbol of Hungarian national resistance and freedom.

events.title: Kádár Era
events.description: Kádár János ruled Hungary 33 years. Initially hated as 'traitor', but gradually gained acceptance through pragmatic policies. From 1960s, Kádár promoted 'Who is not against us is with us' policy, looser than other Eastern European countries. 1968 'New Economic Mechanism' introduced market elements, allowed small private enterprises, improved living standards. Hungary became 'happiest barracks in East', with relative prosperity and freedom (travel, culture). But political dissent not tolerated, secret police surveillance. 1980s economic stagnation, debt increased, reform demands rose.

events.title: Outbreak of 1956 Revolution
events.description: On October 23, 1956, Budapest student demonstration demanding reforms and Soviet withdrawal escalated into national uprising. Protesters toppled Stalin statue, seized radio station. Secret police fired on crowd, uprising became revolution. Workers joined, armed resistance began. October 24, Soviet tanks entered Budapest but encountered fierce resistance. After October 25 Parliament Square massacre, revolution became freedom war. Nagy Imre reinstated as Prime Minister, promising reforms. Revolutionary committees formed nationwide, secret police disbanded. This was greatest challenge to Soviet rule in Eastern Europe during Cold War.

events.title: Peaceful Transition
events.description: In 1988, Kádár forced to retire, reformists took over Communist Party. Gorbachev's reforms and Soviet loosening control encouraged change. In 1989, Hungary experienced rapid peaceful democratic transition: January passed Assembly and Association Act, allowing multi-party system; February acknowledged 1956 Revolution as 'popular uprising' not 'counterrevolution'; June 16 Nagy solemnly reburied, hundreds of thousands attended; June-September Round Table talks negotiated political transition; October amended constitution, declaring multi-party democratic republic; October 23 (1956 Revolution anniversary) proclaimed Third Republic. Most symbolic: May dismantled Iron Curtain with Austria, September allowed East German refugees transit to West, accelerating Eastern European communism collapse.

events.title: First Free Elections
events.description: March-April 1990, Hungary held free elections, first in 45 years. Center-right Hungarian Democratic Forum (MDF) won, Antall József became Prime Minister. Alliance of Free Democrats and Independent Smallholders also entered parliament. Former Communists (renamed Socialist Party) suffered crushing defeat. Hungary peacefully completed transition from communism to democracy, becoming Eastern European model. New government faced daunting tasks: economic transition (from planned to market), privatization, social pains. But democracy consolidated, Hungary moved toward Western integration.

events.title: Economic Transition and Western Integration
events.description: In 1990s, Hungary experienced difficult economic transition: state enterprise privatization, foreign investment introduction, market economy establishment. Initial pains: unemployment, inflation, living standards decline, 'transition fatigue'. But Hungary successfully attracted foreign investment (especially automobile industry), economy gradually recovered. Political stability, peaceful alternation of left-right parties: MDF (1990-94), Socialists (1994-98), Fidesz (1998-2002), Socialists (2002-10). Diplomatic focus Western integration: joined NATO in 1999, EU in 2004, greatest post-communist achievement, marking Hungary 'return to Europe'.
